source.title: Transforming Rank: How Architecture Navigates the Spectral Pathologies of Depth

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains randomly initialized networks on CIFAR-10 and reports test accuracy as a coarse trainability signal, but does not report training classification error or test the specific recipes in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's CIFAR-10 results bear indirectly on whether depth and normalization settings train, but test accuracy cannot establish whether training classification error reaches zero. Initialization rank measurements alone are not training outcomes. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures initialization spectra and best CIFAR-10 test accuracy in residual MLPs. These results do not measure any version's specified effect: training classification error, spurious local minima, plain-network initialization and training speed, stability-threshold loss dynamics, or batch-normalization acceleration. RMSNorm and LayerNorm are explicitly distinguished from BatchNorm.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the CIFAR-10 result if initialization effective rank explicitly means input–output Jacobian rank. The authors' broader conclusion is that skip routing, normalization placement, the second branch matrix, and width expansion preserve different rank objects while trading off rank preservation, layer composition, and parameter count. Representation-rank collapse alone does not prevent their normalized networks from training on CIFAR-10.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies residual MLP feedforward blocks and initialization rank, using CIFAR-10 best test accuracy over Adam learning-rate sweeps. It does not reproduce the versions' specified training-error measurements or recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Normalization placement and operation, initialization scale, depth, and learning rate affect the reported rank or CIFAR-10 test-accuracy outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-Norm residual MLPs achieve 50–57% best CIFAR-10 test accuracy across the tested grid. Post-Norm reaches 18% at initialization scale 1 and depth 192, and chance at depth 384, accompanying input–output Jacobian rank collapse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization input–output Jacobian effective rank predicts coarse CIFAR-10 trainability across normalization placements, initialization scales, and depths in these residual MLPs.

fits_no_version.finding: Without normalization, single- and two-matrix residual MLPs fail by about depths 50 and 100. Pre-RMSNorm restores similar best test accuracies through depth 1000 despite single-matrix representation rank collapsing to approximately two.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-RMSNorm controls magnitude and permits deep residual MLP training on CIFAR-10 despite severe initialization representation-rank collapse.

record.problems: CIFAR-10 is described by the authors as an easy task and the trainability test as coarse. The reported CIFAR outcome is best test accuracy over a learning-rate sweep, not training classification error. The main grid's exact per-cell values are presented as heatmaps rather than transcribed in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Initialization-rank measurements and cited results from other studies are not training outcomes for the claim and are not included.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in convolutional networks; CIFAR-100, corrupted labels, and the specified model-size and training-recipe comparisons.
Teacher-student ReLU local-minimum frequencies and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks versus identity-shortcut counterparts; special plain-tanh initializations and Fixup.
Activation-matched initialization effects on plain-network learning speed and trainable depth; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization and very deep convolutional training.
Loss and curvature dynamics relative to the initial linearized stability limit, catapult recovery, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence below the threshold.
BatchNorm effects on accuracy gain per training time and learning-rate tolerance versus otherwise comparable unnormalized networks; Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: All rows concern related outcomes outside the six versions, so their states are cannot_determine relative to those versions. The maximum stable learning rate in Appendix B.4 is defined by a test-accuracy cutoff, not a curvature-based stability threshold; it does not test V5. No version-relevant missing results were identified.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training classification error, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, SGD, or the version's comparison with smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student experiments or neuron-count sweep.
Does not compare plain batch-normalized convolutional networks with shortcut networks, or test the cited special initializations. Its CIFAR-10 MLP results report test accuracy, not training error.
Does not test activation-matched initialization, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, or 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
Does not test learning rates above a stability limit or report the catapult or edge-of-stability dynamics.
Does not compare batch normalization with no batch normalization in the listed sigmoid, VGG, or Inception settings, or test Fixup.

rows.subject: residual networks with a two-matrix ReLU branch, Pre-Norm
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 across initialization scale and depth grid; reports best test accuracy over a learning-rate sweep.
rows.measure: Best CIFAR-10 test accuracy; paper describes the grid as training successfully across the entire grid.
rows.value: Best test accuracy over the grid is shown in Figure 6; text says training succeeds across the entire grid.
rows.note: This is a test-accuracy-based trainability signal, not a reported training-error measurement. The text says CIFAR-10 is an easy task and calls this a coarse test of whether a configuration trains at all.
rows.check: The reported success concerns best test accuracy, not a claim-version outcome. Figure 6 supplies the grid: initialization scales 0.02–4, depths 12–384, and test accuracies 50–57%.

rows.subject: residual networks with a two-matrix ReLU branch, Post-Norm
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 across initialization scale and depth grid; reports best test accuracy over a learning-rate sweep.
rows.note: The authors say accuracy first drops at this depth; this is test accuracy, not training error.
rows.check: The 18% test accuracy is correctly extracted, but cannot establish a partial effect for any version.

rows.subject: residual networks with a two-matrix ReLU branch, Post-Norm
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 across initialization scale and depth grid; reports best test accuracy over a learning-rate sweep.
rows.note: The authors state that accuracy reaches chance after the initialization rank collapses. Test accuracy does not establish training classification error.
rows.check: Chance test accuracy is correctly extracted, but does not establish absence of any version's effect.

rows.subject: single-matrix ReLU residual network (M=1)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 without normalization; best test accuracy over a learning-rate sweep.
rows.measure: Best CIFAR-10 test accuracy; explicit statement of training failure
rows.value: Fails to train by about depth 50.
rows.note: The paper reports test accuracy as the outcome and separately describes the configuration as failing to train; it does not give its training classification error.
rows.check: The authors' failure description is accurate under their test-accuracy criterion. This residual MLP result does not measure the plain convolutional-network training-error effect in V3.
